claims.text: The dominant mechanism governing improved wear performance in HEA protective coatings is shear-induced formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous surface layer through dynamic amorphization.
Sliding wear generates the ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous surface layer.
The surface layer reduces friction by enabling grain-boundary sliding.
The surface layer suppresses dislocation-driven deformation mechanisms.
Standard deposition can produce a baseline CoCrFeMnNi coating with a nanocrystalline or partially amorphous microstructure and limited predisposition to dynamic amorphization.
Changing deposition temperature or sputtering power modulates the coating's propensity for dynamic amorphization during subsequent wear.
Increasing deposition temperature or sputtering power increases the free energy stored in the coating.
Greater stored free energy makes the coating more susceptible to shear-induced dynamic amorphization.
The ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface state of CoCrFeMnNi exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
Inverse Hall-Petch dynamic softening lowers near-surface shear strength and consequently lowers friction.
Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer is associated with high wear resistance in CoCrFeMnNi.
Deposition conditions favoring dynamic amorphization will produce a thicker and more continuous ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous wear layer than baseline deposition conditions.
Coatings favoring dynamic amorphization will exhibit friction coefficients near 0.2–0.3.
Coatings favoring dynamic amorphization will have lower wear rates than coatings deposited under baseline conditions.
Baseline coatings with less predisposition to dynamic amorphization have higher friction coefficients and wear rates.
The proposed mechanism should apply to compositions similar to CoCrFeMnNi.
Moderate-to-high sliding loads and velocities promote the high-strain-rate shear needed for the proposed microstructural evolution.
Inert or ultra-high-vacuum testing minimizes oxidation and mixed-metal-oxide film formation that can affect friction and wear.
The proposed mechanism may cease to dominate in high-temperature or oxidizing environments because tribochemical effects can dominate.
